summary: A periodic status report summarizing the standardization state of Internet protocols and specifications at that time. It is a snapshot list rather than a protocol specification. It is now historic, and it was replaced by RFC 2600.

plainLanguage.summary: This was a report card listing which internet rules were official and which were still being tried out, as of one moment in time. Newer report cards replaced it.

questions: list of internet standards status in 1999
what internet protocols were standards in 1999
how does the internet standards process work
what is the difference between standard and experimental protocols
subtitle: A snapshot of which Internet protocols were standards, experimental, or historic as of June 1999

tldr.problem: Internet protocols evolve constantly, and there was no single place showing their current maturity level or standardization status at any given moment.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2500 is a status report that lists hundreds of RFC protocol specifications organized by their maturity level: Standard, Draft Standard, Proposed Standard, Experimental, Informational, and Historic categories.
tldr.outcome: This is a periodic snapshot document; newer versions replaced it as new protocols were standardized. RFC 2600 issued a year later became the authoritative list, and continues to be updated every few years.

today: RFC 2500 is Historic; it was replaced by RFC 2600 (June 2000) and is now a snapshot of standardization from 1999. The IETF continues to publish updated protocol status lists (most recently in RFC 9100) to track the evolution of Internet standards.

sections.title: What This Document Is
sections.content:
RFC 2500 is not a protocol specification; it is a status report. Published by the RFC Editor in accordance with RFC 2026 (the Internet Standards Process), it lists the state of all Internet protocol specifications at one point in time: June 1999.

The document collects hundreds of RFCs and sorts them by their standardization level. It serves as the authoritative registry of which protocols are Internet Standards, which are still experimental, which have been replaced by newer versions, and which have been made historic. Organizations and network operators use it to understand which protocols are safe to deploy and which are too immature or deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a big list of all the internet rules, sorted by how official they are. An Internet Standard is like a law everyone follows. Experimental means scientists are still testing it. Historic means it is old and should not be used anymore.

sections.title: Categories of Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC organizes protocols into six main categories. Standard Protocols (like TCP, UDP, IP, and DNS) are stable, well-tested, widely deployed, and required for Internet interoperability. Draft Standard Protocols are further along than proposed standards but not yet full standards. Proposed Standard Protocols (the largest category) are new or revised specifications being evaluated by the IETF.

Experimental Protocols are specifications for novel ideas, often not meant for wide deployment. Historic Protocols are old standards that have been superseded. Informational Protocols are documented for reference but are not on the standards track; this category includes protocols developed by other organizations or examples and case studies.
sections.plainLanguage: A Standard is a rule everyone agrees on and uses. Draft Standard means it is almost ready. Proposed Standard means people are voting on it. Experimental means scientists are testing a new idea. Historic means it is old and replaced. Informational is just information, not an official rule.

sections.title: Internet Standards in June 1999
sections.content:
In June 1999, there were roughly two dozen Internet Standards covering the core Internet services. These include fundamental protocols like IP (RFC 791) and ICMP (RFC 792), transport protocols TCP (RFC 793) and UDP (RFC 768), the DNS (RFC 1034-1035), SMTP for email (RFC 821), FTP for file transfer (RFC 959), and Telnet (RFC 854-855).

The list also includes network-specific standards describing how to run Internet protocols over specific link technologies (Ethernet, token ring, PPP, ATM, and others). The document notes changes from its predecessor, RFC 2400, with an asterisk marking each new or updated entry, showing how the standards landscape evolves continuously.
sections.plainLanguage: The big rules in June 1999 included email (SMTP), web basics (HTTP was not yet on this list as a full standard), file transfer (FTP), and the core internet plumbing (IP and TCP). The document shows how it changed since the previous version.

sections.title: Work in Progress: Proposed and Experimental Protocols
sections.content:
The largest sections list Proposed Standard Protocols (over 300 RFCs) and Experimental Protocols (over 100). The Proposed Standard list includes early versions of protocols that later became standards, such as IPv6 (RFC 2460), DHCP (RFC 2131), SNMP v3, and HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2068, then later RFC 2616).

The Experimental list shows the breadth of Internet research: novel multicast methods, new security schemes, extensions for performance, and protocols for specialized use cases like mobile IP and stream protocols. Most experimental RFCs never become standards, but some of the most important Internet protocols started here.
sections.plainLanguage: Proposed Standards are ideas that people are voting on to make official. Experimental are wild ideas scientists are trying out. Most experiments fail, but some become the internet rules everyone uses.

sections.title: The Standardization Process and Historic Protocols
sections.content:
RFC 2500 reflects the Internet Standards Process described in RFC 2026: a protocol must move through Proposed, then Draft, then Standard status as it gains maturity and support. The Historic Protocols section lists specifications that have been obsoleted or superseded—for instance, older versions of SNMP or routing protocols replaced by newer designs.

The document notes there are also Applicability Statements—RFCs that clarify when and how to use a standard, especially important for protocols like OSPF and RIPng where multiple competing implementations exist. The snapshot shows the state of Internet standardization effort at a moment when IPv6 and modern security protocols (IPsec, TLS) were still being finalized.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols move from new ideas (Proposed) to widely used (Standard). When something better comes along, the old one becomes Historic. Some RFCs just explain when you should use a protocol.
